exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 1 and 2, compute each matrix sum or product if it is defined. If an expression is undefined, explain why. Let
In the rest of this exercise set and in those to follow, you should assume that each matrix expression is defined. That is, the sizes of the matrices (and vectors) involved “match” appropriately.

problem.paragraph: Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & {- 1} \\ 5 & {- 2} \end{bmatrix}$$ . Compute $$3I_{2} - A$$ and $$(3I_{2})A$$ .﻿
Compute $$A - 5I_{3}$$ and $$\left( 5I_{3} \right)A$$ , when $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & - 1 & 3 \\ - 8 & 7 & - 3 \\ - 4 & 1 & 8 \end{bmatrix} .$$

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 5 and 6, compute the product $$AB$$ in two ways: (a) by the definition, where $$A\textbf{b}_{1}$$ and $$A\textbf{b}_{2}$$ are computed separately, and (b) by the row–column rule for computing $$AB$$ .

problem.paragraph: $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} {- 1} & 2 \\ 5 & 4 \\ 2 & {- 3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 3 & {- 4} \\ {- 2} & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ ﻿
$$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 4 & {- 2} \\ {- 3} & 0 \\ 3 & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & 3 \\ 4 & {- 1} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ ﻿
If a matrix $$A$$ is $$5 \times 3$$ and the product $$AB$$ is $$5 \times 7$$ , what is the size of $$B$$ ?
How many rows does $$B$$ have if $$BC$$ is a $$3 \times 4$$ matrix?

Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 2 & 5 \\ {- 3} & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 4 & {- 5} \\ 3 & k \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . What value(s) of $$k$$ , if any, will make $$AB = BA$$ ?

Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 2 & {- 3} \\ {- 4} & 6 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 8 & 4 \\ 5 & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , and $$C = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 5 & {- 2} \\ 3 & 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Verify that $$AB = AC$$ and yet $$B \neq C$$ .﻿

Let $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 4 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ and $$D = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Compute $$AD$$ and $$DA$$ . Explain how the columns or rows of $$A$$ change when $$A$$ is multiplied by $$D$$ on the right or on the left. Find a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix $$B$$ , not the identity matrix or the zero matrix, such that $$AB = BA$$ .﻿

Let $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 3 & {- 6} \\ {- 1} & 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Construct a $$2 \times 2$$ matrix $$B$$ such that $$AB$$ is the zero matrix. Use two different nonzero columns for $$B$$ .﻿

Let $$\textbf{r}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{r}_{p}$$ be vectors in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , and let $$Q$$ be an $$m \times n$$ matrix. Write the matrix $$\begin{bmatrix} {Q\textbf{r}_{1}\cdots Q\textbf{r}_{p}} \end{bmatrix}$$ as a product of two matrices (neither of which is an identity matrix).

Let $$U$$ be the $$3 \times 2$$ cost matrix described in Example 6 of Section 1.8. The first column of $$U$$ lists the costs per dollar of output for manufacturing product $$B$$ , and the second column lists the costs per dollar of output for product $$C$$ . (The costs are categorized as materials, labor, and overhead.) Let $$\textbf{q}_{1}$$ be a vector in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{2}$$ that lists the output (measured in dollars) of products $$B$$ and $$C$$ manufactured during the first quarter of the year, and let $$\textbf{q}_{2}$$ , $$\textbf{q}_{3}$$ , and $$\textbf{q}_{4}$$ be the analogous vectors that list the amounts of products $$B$$ and $$C$$ manufactured in the second, third, and fourth quarters, respectively. Give an economic description of the data in the matrix $$UQ$$ , where $$Q = \left\lbrack \textbf{q}_{1} \textbf{q}_{2} \textbf{q}_{3} \textbf{q}_{4} \right\rbrack$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: Exercises 15–24 concern arbitrary matrices $$A$$ , $$B$$ , and $$C$$ for which the indicated sums and products are defined. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$2 \times 2$$ with columns $$\textbf{a}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{a}_{2}$$ , and $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ , $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , respectively, then $$AB = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{ll} {\mathbf{a}_{1}\mathbf{b}_{1}} & {\mathbf{a}_{2}\mathbf{b}_{2}} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .﻿

(T/F) If $$A$$ and $$B$$ are $$3 \times 3$$ and $$B = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{lll} \mathbf{b}_{1} & \mathbf{b}_{2} & \mathbf{b}_{3} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , then $$AB = \lbrack A\textbf{b}_{1} + A\textbf{b}_{2} + A\textbf{b}_{3}\rbrack$$ .﻿
(T/F) Each column of $$AB$$ is a linear combination of the columns of $$B$$ using weights from the corresponding column of $$A$$ .﻿
(T/F) The second row of $$AB$$ is the second row of $$A$$ multiplied on the right by $$B$$ .﻿
(T/F) $$AB + AC = A(B + C)$$ ﻿
(T/F) The transpose of a product of matrices equals the product of their transposes in the same order.
(T/F) The transpose of a sum of matrices equals the sum of their transposes.

If $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & {- 2} \\ {- 2} & 5 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$AB = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} {- 1} & 2 & {- 1} \\ 6 & {- 9} & 3 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ , determine the first and second columns of $$B$$ .﻿
Suppose the first two columns, $$\textbf{b}_{1}$$ and $$\textbf{b}_{2}$$ , of $$B$$ are equal. What can you say about the columns of $$AB$$ (if $$AB$$ is defined)? Why?
Suppose the third column of $$B$$ is the sum of the first two columns. What can you say about the third column of $$AB$$ ? Why?
Suppose the second column of $$B$$ is all zeros. What can you say about the second column of $$AB$$ ?
Suppose the last column of $$AB$$ is all zeros, but $$B$$ itself has no column of zeros. What can you say about the columns of $$A$$ ?
Show that if the columns of $$B$$ are linearly dependent, then so are the columns of $$AB$$ .
Suppose $$CA = I_{n}$$ (the $$n \times n$$ identity matrix). Show that the equation $${A\textbf{x}} = \textbf{0}$$ has only the trivial solution. Explain why $$A$$ cannot have more columns than rows.

Suppose $$AD = I_{m}$$ (the $$m \times m$$ identity matrix). Show that for any $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ , the equation $$A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$$ has a solution. [Hint: Think about the equation $$AD\textbf{b} = \textbf{b}$$ .] Explain why $$A$$ cannot have more rows than columns.

Suppose $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix and there exist $$n \times m$$ matrices $$C$$ and $$D$$ such that $$CA = I_{n}$$ and $$AD = I_{m}$$ . Prove that $$m = n$$ and $$C = D$$ . [Hint: Think about the product $$CAD$$ .]
Suppose $$A$$ is a $$3 \times n$$ matrix whose columns span $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$$ . Explain how to construct an $$n \times 3$$ matrix $$D$$ such that $$AD = I_{3}$$ .﻿

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 35 and 36, view vectors in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ as $$n \times 1$$ matrices. For $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , the matrix product $$\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{v}$$ is a $$1 \times 1$$ matrix, called the scalar product, or inner product, of $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . It is usually written as a single real number without brackets. The matrix product $$\textbf{uv}^{T}$$ is an $$n \times n$$ ﻿ matrix, called the ﻿outer product﻿ of $$\textbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . The products $$\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{v}$$ and $$\textbf{u}\textbf{v}^{T}$$ will appear later in the text.

problem.paragraph: Let $$\textbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 2} \\ 3 \\ {- 4} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\textbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c \end{bmatrix}$$ . Compute $$\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{v}$$ , $$\textbf{v}^{T}\textbf{u}$$ , $$\textbf{uv}^{T}$$ , and $$\textbf{v}\textbf{u}^{T}$$ .﻿

If $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ are in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ , how are $$\textbf{u}^{T}\textbf{v}$$ and $$\textbf{v}^{T}\textbf{u}$$ related? How are $$\textbf{u}\textbf{v}^{T}$$ and $$\textbf{v}\textbf{u}^{T}$$ related?

Prove Theorem 2(b) and 2(c). Use the row–column rule. The $$(i,j) \text{-entry}$$ in $$A(B + C)$$ can be written as $$a_{i 1} ( b_{1 j} + c_{1 j} ) + \hdots + a_{i n} ( b_{n j} + c_{n j} ) \text{or} \sum_{k = 1}^{n} a_{i k} ( b_{k j} + c_{k j} )$$
Prove Theorem 2(d). [Hint: The $$(i,j) \text{-entry}$$ in $$(rA)B$$ is $$(ra_{i1})b_{1j} + \cdots + (ra_{in})b_{nj}$$ .]﻿
Show that $$I_{m}A = A$$ when $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix. You can assume $$I_{m}\textbf{x} = \textbf{x}$$ for all $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ .﻿
Show that $$AI_{n} = A$$ when $$A$$ is an $$m \times n$$ matrix. [Hint: Use the (column) definition of $$AI_{n}$$ .]﻿
Prove Theorem 3(d). [Hint: Consider the $$j \text{th}$$ row of $$\left. (AB \right)^{T}$$ .]﻿
Give a formula for $$\left. (AB\textbf{x} \right)^{T}$$ , where $$\mathbf{x}$$ is a vector and $$A$$ and $$B$$ are matrices of appropriate sizes.

exercise_group.instruction: A useful way to test new ideas in matrix algebra, or to make conjectures, is to make calculations with matrices selected at random. Checking a property for a few matrices does not prove that the property holds in general, but it makes the property more believable. Also, if the property is actually false, you may discover this when you make a few calculations.

problem.paragraph: [T] Write the command(s) that will create a $$6 \times 4$$ matrix with random entries. In what range of numbers do the entries lie? Tell how to create a $$3 \times 3$$ matrix with random integer entries between $$- 9$$ and $$9$$ . [Hint: If $$x$$ is a random number such that $$0 < x < 1$$ , then $$- 9.5 < 19(x - .5) < 9.5$$ .]﻿

[T] Construct a random $$4 \times 4$$ matrix $$A$$ and test whether $$\left(\right. A + I \left.\right)$$ $$(A - I) = A^{2} - I$$ . The best way to do this is to compute $$(A + I)(A - I) - (A^{2} - I)$$ and verify that this difference is the zero matrix. Do this for three random matrices. Then test $$(A + B)(A - B) = A^{2} - B^{2}$$ the same way for three pairs of random $$4 \times 4$$ matrices. Report your conclusions.

[T] Use at least three pairs of random $$4 \times 4$$ matrices $$A$$ and $$B$$ to test the equalities $${(A + B)^{T}} = A^{T} + B^{T}$$ and $${(AB)^{T}} = A^{T}B^{T}$$ . (See Exercise 45.) Report your conclusions. [Note: Most matrix programs use $$A\prime$$ for $$A^{T}$$ .]﻿
Compute $$S^{k}$$ for $$k = 2,\ldots,6$$ .﻿

[T] Describe in words what happens when you compute $$A^{5}$$ , $$A^{10}$$ , $$A^{20}$$ , and $$A^{30}$$ for $$A = \begin{bmatrix} 1 / 6 & 1 / 2 & 1 / 3 \\ 1 / 2 & 1 / 4 & 1 / 4 \\ 1 / 3 & 1 / 4 & 5 / 12 \end{bmatrix}$$

[T] The matrix $$M$$ can detect a particular $$2 \times 2$$ colored pattern like in Example 9. Create a nonzero $$4 \times 1$$ vector $$\textbf{x}$$ by choosing each entry to be a zero or one. Test to see if $$\textbf{x}$$ corresponds to the right pattern by calculating $$\textbf{x}^{T}M\textbf{x}$$ . $$A\textbf{x} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rr} 1 & {- 3} \\ {- 2} & 4 \end{array} \right\rbrack\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} {- 4} \\ 2 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . So $$(A\textbf{x})^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} {- 4} & 2 \end{bmatrix}$$ . Also, $$\mathbf{x}^{T} A^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 2 \\ - 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} - 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix} .$$

The quantities $$(A\textbf{x})^{T}$$ and $$\textbf{x}^{T} A^{T}$$ are equal, by Theorem 3(d). Next, $$\mathbf{xx}^{T} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}5 \\ 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}5 & 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}25 & 15 \\ 15 & 9\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \mathbf{x}^{T} \mathbf{x} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}5 & 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}5 \\ 3\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}25 + 9\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} = 34$$

A $$1 \times 1$$ matrix such as $$\textbf{x}^{T}\textbf{x}$$ is usually written without the brackets. Finally, $$A^{T}\textbf{x}^{T}$$ is not defined, because $$\textbf{x}^{T}$$ does not have two rows to match the two columns of $$A^{T}$$ .﻿

The fastest way to compute $$A^{2}\textbf{x}$$ is to compute $$A(A\textbf{x})$$ . The product $$A\textbf{x}$$ requires $$16$$ multiplications, $$4$$ for each entry, and $$A(A\textbf{x})$$ requires $$16$$ more. In contrast, the product $$A^{2}$$ requires $$64$$ multiplications, $$4$$ for each of the $$16$$ entries in $$A^{2}$$ After that, $$A^{2}\textbf{x}$$ takes $$16$$ more multiplications, for a total of $$80$$ .

First observe that by the definition of matrix multiplication, $$A B & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}A b_{1} & A b_{2} & \hdots & A b_{n}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} & = & \begin{bmatrix} \begin{matrix}A b_{1} & A b_{1} & \hdots & A b_{1}\end{matrix} \end{bmatrix} ,$$

so the columns of $$AB$$ are identical. Next, recall that $${ \text{r} \text{o} } \text{w} _{i}(AB) = { \text{r} \text{o} } \text{w} _{i}(A) \cdot B$$ . Since all the rows of $$A$$ are identical, all the rows of $$AB$$ are identical. Putting this information about the rows and columns together, it follows that all the entries in $$AB$$ are the same.
